title: Natural stone, wood veneer, brass: materials of a luxury interior
seo_title: Stone, Veneer, Brass: Luxury Interior Materials
description: Luxury interior materials explained: natural stone, wood veneer, solid wood and brass — where to use them, what to replace them with, how to combine and care for them.
lead: Natural stone, wood veneer and brass are the materials that most often make an interior feel luxurious. Each has its own character: stone absorbs stains, veneer dislikes dry air and brass changes colour. Here is where these materials work best, what can replace them and how to combine them so the interior only gets better with age.

body: Why materials define the level of an interior

Two interiors with the same layout and furniture can look completely different because of their materials. Real stone has depth and veining that no print can reproduce. Veneer shows the living grain of the wood. Brass reflects light warmly and develops a noble tone over time. These materials feel good to the touch and, most importantly, they age well: wear and patina add character instead of looking like damage.

At the same time, natural materials demand know-how. They have to be chosen for the specific place, installed correctly and maintained. A mistake anywhere in that chain and an expensive material looks worse than a good imitation. That is why we decide on stone, wood and metal at the design stage — together with lighting, details and budget — and not in a showroom after the renovation has started.
Natural stone: marble, travertine, granite, quartzite

Stone is the strongest accent in a luxury interior, but different types behave differently. Marble and travertine are beautiful and warm, yet relatively soft and porous: they absorb liquids and etch from acids such as lemon juice, wine and vinegar. Granite and quartzite are harder and more durable, so they suit kitchen worktops and heavily used floors better.
marble — bathrooms, walls, fireplace surrounds, tables, feature panels
travertine — floors, walls, bathtubs, furniture; pores are usually filled or left as texture
granite and quartzite — kitchen worktops, window sills, stairs, high-traffic floors
any natural stone needs a protective sealer that is renewed periodically

Another point: every slab is unique. When a wall or island needs several slabs, the pattern is matched in advance, sometimes book-matched so the veins continue. So stone is selected from actual slabs, not from a catalogue sample, and the layout is approved before cutting.
Linden Penthouse living room with walnut veneer walls, a marble column, a TV on a stand and a rug
Linden Penthouse: walnut veneer and marble — warm and cool in balance

Large-format stone-look porcelain is very convincing today: it does not stain, it is lighter and it costs less. It makes sense on large floor areas, in showers, on kitchen splashbacks and in commercial spaces. Keep natural stone where people see and touch it: the island, the bathtub, the fireplace, a table, a feature wall. This combination gives the feel of a genuine material without the risks or unnecessary cost. Just avoid mixing natural stone and an imitation of the same type in one room — side by side the difference shows.

The bathroom is where natural stone looks most luxurious and works in the toughest conditions: water, soap, cosmetics, temperature changes. Proper sealing, good joints and well-planned ventilation matter here. Stone on walls and monolithic basins will last for years, while for a shower floor anti-slip porcelain is often more practical. Plumbing details are planned separately: openings for taps and drains are cut to the drawings before installation.
Veneer and solid wood: the warmth of timber

Veneer is a thin layer of natural wood bonded to a stable core. That is why veneered panels and fronts do not warp the way solid wood does and can be made in large sizes: floor-to-ceiling wall panels, flush doors, kitchen and wardrobe fronts. In a luxury interior leaf matching is key: the grain should flow across adjacent panels and the tone should be consistent over the whole surface.
walnut — a deep, warm tone; a classic for living rooms, studies and bedrooms
oak — versatile, pairs well with stone and metal
ash — light, with expressive grain, for Scandinavian and contemporary interiors

The finish changes the character of the wood: oil keeps a natural look and is easy to touch up locally, lacquer protects better against moisture and stains. Remember that wood reacts to humidity and sunlight: heated rooms need humidity control, and veneer in direct sun changes tone over time.

Solid wood belongs where timber works structurally and is touched: dining tables, stairs, window sills, handles, slatted panels. It can be fully refinished — scratches are sanded out — but it moves with humidity, so it needs the right fixing details.

Brass brings warmth and light to an interior. It is used in light fittings, taps, handles, trims and decorative inlays in stone and wood. It is important to understand the finishes. Lacquered brass keeps its original shine for a long time. Unlacquered brass is a living material: it darkens and develops a patina that you can keep as character or polish periodically. For taps and shower systems a PVD brushed-brass finish is often chosen — it is more resistant to water and cleaning products.
one or two metals in an interior, not five different tones
brass in repeating details: lighting, handles, taps
a brushed surface shows fingerprints less than a polished one
Yacht VIP living room with a textured stone wall, lit niches, a fireplace and wooden tables
Yacht VIP: textured stone, wood and warm light — an interior that ages well
Lighting decides how a material looks

The same marble looks grey and flat under cool light and deep and soft under warm light. Veneer loses its texture under direct overhead light but shows its grain under side or concealed lighting. Brass only comes alive when it has something to reflect. That is why we approve materials and lighting together: colour temperature, fixture positions and niche lighting are chosen for the palette, not the other way round.

A luxury interior rarely uses a dozen materials. Usually there are three or four main ones — for example light stone, walnut veneer, brass and textiles — repeated across different rooms. That repetition creates coherence. Contrasts work well: cool stone and warm wood, matt and gloss, smooth and textured.
choose a base palette of three or four materials
gather the samples in one place and view them in daylight and in the evening
decide on the accent points where the most expensive material works
repeat materials across several zones for coherence
record everything in a specification with product codes

Natural materials need simple but regular care. Stone — neutral, acid-free cleaners and renewed sealing. Wood — moderate humidity, gentle products and, if needed, a fresh coat of oil. Brass — a soft cloth and no abrasives or harsh chemicals. Pass these rules on to whoever does the cleaning: most damage comes from the wrong products.

In our interior design projects materials are approved from physical samples, not on screen: we assemble the palette, show it under different lighting and record product codes in the specification. faq: Is marble suitable for a kitchen worktop?
It can be used, but marble is soft and reacts to acids, leaving dull marks. For a busy kitchen granite, quartzite or porcelain are more practical; keep marble for the island or an accent.
Why choose veneer over solid wood?
Veneer is more stable: large panels and fronts do not warp with humidity. Solid wood suits tables, stairs and frequently touched details because it can be sanded and refinished.
Brass darkens over time — is that normal?
Unlacquered brass naturally develops a patina. If you want a consistent look, choose lacquered brass or a PVD finish.
How many materials should one interior use?
Usually three or four main materials repeated across different rooms. That keeps the interior coherent.
